lessons.briefing:
MISSION BRIEFING: You are a Rebuilder Corps recruit. The Blackout of 2031 showed the world what happens when digital infrastructure collapses. Your first mission is to understand the five invisible layers that modern society depends on — so you know exactly what you are defending.

Modern society runs on five invisible layers: (1) Power grids — electricity is the foundation; without it nothing else works. (2) Communications networks — fibre, satellite, and mobile towers that carry data. (3) Computing systems — the servers, routers, and devices that process information. (4) Databases — the stored records of money, health, identity, and logistics. (5) Applications — the software that citizens and businesses use every day. When any layer fails, everything above it fails too. The Blackout of 2031 proved this in 72 hours: attackers hit the power grid and communications layer simultaneously, and within three days banking, hospitals, and supply chains collapsed across East Africa. Rebuilder Corps exists to prevent it happening again.

Jamii ya kisasa inategemea tabaka tano zisizoonekana: (1) Gridi za umeme — msingi wa kila kitu. (2) Mitandao ya mawasiliano — nyuzi macho, setilaiti, na minara. (3) Mifumo ya kompyuta — seva na vifaa vinavyochakata data. (4) Hifadhidata — kumbukumbu za fedha, afya, na utambulisho. (5) Programu — zinazotumika na raia na biashara kila siku. Tabaka moja likiporomoka, yaliyopo juu yake yanaporomoka pia.

lessons.title: What is Digital Infrastructure?

lessons.briefing:
MISSION BRIEFING: Modern life does not just use the internet — it is built on top of it. In this mission, examine what happens when digital connectivity is severed.

Every critical public system in East Africa relies on communications networks to operate: (1) Healthcare — hospitals verify health insurance, retrieve digital laboratory tests, and coordinate emergency ambulances across optical and wireless links. (2) Clean Water & Utilities — municipal water treatment plants and electric substations use telemetry and remote sensors to monitor pressure, chlorination, and load. (3) Commerce & Banking — M-Pesa, debit card terminals, and interbank clearance depend on secure cellular packet data. (4) Supply Chains — food transport, fuel distribution, and cargo tracking through the Port of Mombasa coordinate through digital manifests.

When network infrastructure is disrupted, the impact cascades: if payment systems fail, citizens cannot buy fuel; without fuel, backup hospital generators stop; without power, water pumps run dry. Network defense is not just IT — it is public safety.

lessons.title: How Civilisation Depends on Networks

lessons.briefing:
Three real-world cyberattacks prove that infrastructure attacks are not science fiction — they happened, and they will happen again without defenders.

Case Study 1 — Ukraine Power Grid (2016): Attackers from the Sandworm group compromised SCADA (industrial control) systems at three Ukrainian power distribution companies using spear-phishing emails. They then remotely opened circuit breakers, cutting electricity to approximately 230,000 people in winter. The lesson: critical infrastructure control systems are reachable from the internet and must be isolated and monitored.

Case Study 2 — Colonial Pipeline Ransomware (2021): A single compromised VPN password (found in a leaked credentials database) allowed the DarkSide group to access Colonial Pipeline's IT network. They deployed ransomware that paralysed billing and management systems. Colonial voluntarily shut down its 8,850-km pipeline, disrupting fuel supply to the US East Coast for six days. The lesson: one reused password on an internet-facing system can take down national fuel infrastructure.

Case Study 3 — MOVEit Breaches (2023): The Cl0p ransomware group exploited a zero-day SQL injection vulnerability in the MOVEit file-transfer software used by hundreds of organisations worldwide, including African financial institutions and pension funds. Personal and financial data from millions of people was exfiltrated. The lesson: supply-chain software vulnerabilities affect every organisation that uses the same product — attackers do not need to target you directly.
lessons.briefingSw:

Masimulizi 2 — Colonial Pipeline 2021: Nenosiri moja lililokuwa kwenye orodha ya data zilizovuja liliruhusu wavamizi kueneza ransomware na kusimamisha mabomba ya mafuta kwa siku sita.

Masimulizi 3 — MOVEit 2023: Udhaifu wa SQL injection kwenye programu ya MOVEit uliathiri taasisi nyingi za fedha Afrika na kwingineko.

lessons.title: Real Blackouts: 3 Case Studies
lessons.titleSw: Masimulizi ya kweli ya kukatiwa umeme

lessons.briefing:
Understanding how attackers operate is the first step to stopping them. Every significant cyberattack follows a similar four-phase pattern.

Phase 1 — Reconnaissance: Attackers gather information about their target before striking. They map IP ranges, identify software versions, scrape employee names from LinkedIn, and look for leaked credentials online. This phase is mostly passive and hard to detect.

Phase 2 — Initial Access: Attackers exploit a weakness to get their first foothold inside the target. The three most common vectors are: (a) Phishing — tricking a person into clicking a link or opening an attachment; (b) Unpatched software — exploiting a known vulnerability in outdated systems; (c) Weak or stolen passwords — credential stuffing or brute force. The Nullers sent 40,000 phishing emails during The Blackout. Twelve people clicked. That was enough.

Phase 3 — Persistence: Once inside, attackers install a backdoor or create hidden accounts so they can return even if their initial access method is discovered and closed. They may stay dormant for weeks or months before acting.

Phase 4 — Impact: The final phase is the attacker's goal: steal data, encrypt files for ransom, destroy systems, or use compromised infrastructure to launch attacks elsewhere. The Nullers used all four phases methodically in the months before The Blackout struck.
lessons.briefingSw:
Kuelewa jinsi wavamizi wanavyofanya kazi ni hatua ya kwanza ya kuwazuia. Kila shambulio kubwa linafuata mfumo wa hatua nne.

Hatua 1 — Upelelezi: Kukusanya habari kuhusu lengo kabla ya kushambulia.
Hatua 2 — Uingiaji wa Awali: Kutumia udhaifu kupata nafasi ya kwanza ndani ya mfumo — kupitia udanganyifu, programu isiyosasishwa, au nenosiri dhaifu.
Hatua 3 — Kudumu: Kusakinisha mlango wa siri ili waweze kurudi hata baada ya kugundulika.
Hatua 4 — Athari: Lengo la mwisho — kuiba data, kusimba faili kwa fidia, au kuharibu mifumo.

exercises.explanation: Persistence is Phase 3. After gaining initial access, attackers create mechanisms — backdoors, hidden admin accounts, scheduled tasks — that keep them inside even if their original entry point is closed.

lessons.title: How Cyberattacks Work
lessons.titleSw: Jinsi mashambulizi ya mtandao yanavyofanya kazi

lessons.briefing:
MISSION BRIEFING: Cyberattacks are not abstract lines of code on a terminal screen. They have real human consequences. Step into the shoes of the medical response team at Nakuru Level 5 Hospital during The Blackout of 2031.

At 14:15 on Day 1 of The Blackout, hospital power flickered and transferred to emergency generators. Simultaneously, external broadband, cellular signals, and the centralized hospital management system went dark. Within 30 minutes:
- Patient records, allergy histories, and active medication orders were inaccessible.
- Digital blood bank inventory counts were offline; nurses had to manually count units by flashlight.
- Vaccine cold-chain refrigerators (+2°C to +8°C) were dependent on limited on-site fuel reserves.
- Incoming road trauma referrals could not be coordinated by phone or WhatsApp.

The decisions made in those 72 hours saved lives through disciplined emergency procedures, manual triage tags, and analog VHF radio coordination. Security defenders do not protect machines — they protect human life.

lessons.briefing:
MISSION BRIEFING: In popular media, hackers are often romanticised as lone geniuses in dark rooms. In reality, destruction is easy — construction and defense require true expertise, stamina, and purpose.

The core challenge in cybersecurity is known as the Defender's Dilemma (asymmetric advantage): an adversary only needs to find one unpatched flaw, one stolen password, or one distracted user to breach a network. A defender, by contrast, must protect every server, every workstation, every mobile phone, and every employee, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

Yet defenders hold the decisive long-term advantage: community, collective intelligence, and purpose. When the Rebuilder Corps shares threat intelligence, fixes vulnerabilities, and educates colleagues, we build collective immunity. An attack lasts hours; a fortified infrastructure protects generations. You are training to become a defender of our shared society.

lessons.title: Why Defenders Matter More Than Attackers
lessons.titleSw: Kwa Nini Walinzi Ni Muhimu Zaidi ya Wavamizi

lessons.briefing:
Passwords are the first line of defence for every digital account. Most successful attacks exploit weak or reused passwords — not sophisticated zero-days.

What makes a password strong? Length is the single most important factor. A 14-character password takes vastly longer to crack than an 8-character one, even if the shorter one uses symbols. Aim for 14 or more characters. Uniqueness matters just as much: every account must have a different password. If one account is breached, attackers immediately try the same credentials everywhere else — this is called credential stuffing. Passphrases are the practical solution: three or more random words combined with numbers (e.g. "mango-cloud-47-river") are long, memorable, and strong.

Password managers (like Bitwarden, 1Password, or the built-in manager in your phone) store hundreds of unique, randomly generated passwords behind a single master passphrase. You only need to remember one strong passphrase. The manager does the rest.

Never reuse a password. Never share a password. Change a password immediately if you suspect a breach. These three rules would have prevented the Colonial Pipeline attack.

Nywila ni ulinzi wa kwanza wa kila akaunti ya kidijitali. Mashambulizi mengi yanafanikiwa kwa sababu ya nywila dhaifu au zinazotumiwa tena.

lessons.title: Your Password Is Your Key

lessons.briefing:
Phishing is the number one attack vector globally — and the one that started The Blackout. Attackers send fake emails or SMS messages pretending to be trusted organisations: Safaricom, KCB, the Kenya Revenue Authority, government ministries, or employers.

The six warning signs of phishing:
1. Urgency — "Your account will be closed in 10 minutes unless you act now." Legitimate organisations do not use countdown pressure.
2. Lookalike domains — rebu1ld.ke (the digit 1 replacing the letter l) vs rebuild.ke. Check the sender address carefully.
3. Requests for passwords or OTPs — No legitimate bank, telco, or government agency will ask you to send your password or OTP via email or WhatsApp.
4. Unexpected attachments — A PDF or Word document you did not ask for, especially with a vague name like "salary_slip.pdf".
5. Generic greetings — "Dear Customer" instead of your name.
6. Mismatched links — The displayed URL says one thing but hovering shows a different destination.

The Nullers sent 40,000 phishing emails the morning of The Blackout. The messages pretended to be from the Kenya Power emergency maintenance team. Twelve people clicked. That was enough to give the attackers their initial foothold in the power grid control network.
lessons.briefingSw:
Udanganyifu wa phishing ndiyo njia kuu ya shambulio duniani kote — na ile iliyoanzisha Giza Kuu.

Ishara sita za phishing: (1) Haraka — "Akaunti yako itafungwa dakika 10." (2) Vikoa vinavyofanana — rebu1ld.ke badala ya rebuild.ke. (3) Maombi ya nywila au OTP. (4) Viambatisho visivyotarajiwa. (5) Salamu za jumla — "Mteja Mpendwa." (6) Viungo visivyolingana na maandishi.

Nullers walituma barua pepe 40,000 za udanganyifu siku ya Giza Kuu. Watu 12 walibonyeza. Hiyo ilikuwa ya kutosha.

exercises.explanation: This SMS has multiple red flags: artificial urgency ("15 minutes"), a lookalike domain ("safar1com" with a digit 1), and a non-official link. Safaricom uses official shortcodes and never suspends lines via SMS link. Always verify through the official app or *100#.
exercises.hint: Urgency + suspicious domain = phishing. Always use official channels.

options.text: Tap the link immediately to avoid losing your number
Forward it to a friend to check if it is real
Delete the SMS and verify your account status by dialling *100# or calling the official Safaricom line
Reply with your ID number to prove your identity

exercises.prompt: You receive an SMS: "URGENT: Your Safaricom line will be permanently suspended in 15 minutes. Tap this link to verify your identity: safar1com-verify.link/ke". What should you do?

exercises.explanation: Domain spoofing (also called typosquatting or lookalike domains) is the technique of registering domains that are visually similar to legitimate ones. Users who glance quickly at the URL may not notice the substitution of a digit for a letter.
exercises.hint: The fake domain impersonates the real one visually.
exercises.prompt: An attacker registers the domain "rebu1ld.ke" (using the digit 1 instead of the letter l) to trick Rebuilder Corps staff. This technique of creating domains that closely resemble legitimate ones is called domain ___.

exercises.explanation: Unexpected attachments are a classic phishing vector, especially when they reference high-interest topics like payroll. Verify with the claimed sender through a completely separate channel (a phone call, not a reply to the same email) before opening.
exercises.hint: Verify unexpected attachments through a different channel.

options.text: Open the file — it is probably a genuine HR document
Open it only if your antivirus is running
Contact HR through a separate trusted channel (phone or in-person) to confirm they sent it before opening

exercises.prompt: You receive a work email with an attachment called "Q3_Payroll_Final.xlsx" from your HR department. You were NOT expecting any payroll file today. What is the SAFEST action?

exercises.explanation: Legitimate financial institutions and telcos design their systems so that staff never need — and can never ask for — your PIN or OTP. These are your secrets alone. Any request for them, from any channel, is a social-engineering attack.
exercises.hint: If anyone asks for your PIN or OTP, it is a scam.

lessons.briefing:
MISSION BRIEFING: Attackers rarely invent brand-new zero-day exploits. The overwhelming majority of real-world breaches exploit known vulnerabilities that vendors had already patched months earlier. Your mission is to master patch management.

When security researchers or software engineers discover a bug in an operating system, app, or router firmware, the vendor creates a "patch" (software update) and assigns it a CVE identifier (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, e.g. CVE-2024-38077). Once a patch is announced publicly, malicious actors reverse-engineer the fix and unleash automated scanner bots across the internet, looking for any unpatched device.

If your phone, Wi-Fi router, or server has not installed the update, you become an effortless target. Developing a "patch culture" means:
1. Enabling automatic updates on your mobile operating system and browser.
2. Regularly rebooting devices so updates take effect.
3. Updating firmware on Wi-Fi routers and security cameras, not just phones.
4. Retiring software that is no longer supported with security updates (End-of-Life).

MISSION BRIEFING: There are two types of computer users: those who have experienced catastrophic data loss, and those who are about to. In the Rebuilder Corps, our rule is simple: data that does not exist in three places does not exist.

The gold standard of resilient digital survival is the 3-2-1 Backup Rule:
- 3 Copies of all critical data (1 primary operational copy + 2 backup copies).
- 2 Different Media types (e.g. your computer's internal drive + an external USB drive, or magnetic tape + cloud storage).
- 1 Copy stored Offsite or Offline (air-gapped and disconnected from your local network).

Why must one copy be offline? Modern ransomware specifically searches your local network for connected backup drives, shared network folders (NAS), and cloud sync folders — and encrypts them first so you cannot recover. An air-gapped drive kept in a drawer or an immutable cloud vault with write-once protection is immune to ransomware encryption. Backups turn a catastrophic extortion incident into an afternoon of restoration.

lessons.briefing:
Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) means that logging in requires BOTH something you know (your password) AND something you have (your phone, an authenticator app, or a hardware key). Even if an attacker steals or guesses your password, they still cannot log in without the second factor.

The three types of 2FA, ordered from weakest to strongest:

1. SMS OTP (One-Time Password) — A code sent to your phone via text message. Weak but still far better than a password alone. Vulnerable to SIM-swap attacks, where an attacker convinces your carrier to transfer your number to their SIM card.

2. Authenticator App — Apps like Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, or Authy generate time-based codes that change every 30 seconds. These are not sent over SMS, so SIM-swap attacks do not work. Strong.

3. Hardware Key — Physical devices like YubiKey that plug into USB or tap via NFC. Cryptographically verify you are on the real website (preventing phishing). Strongest protection available.

Enable 2FA on: your email (the master key to all accounts), M-Pesa and banking apps, social media accounts, and any work system that supports it. If your email is protected by 2FA, attackers cannot use the "Forgot Password" link to take over your other accounts — even if they know your email password.

Aina tatu za 2FA kwa nguvu inayoongezeka:
1. OTP ya SMS — Nambari inayotumwa kwa ujumbe mfupi. Dhaifu kidogo lakini bora kuliko nywila peke yake.
2. Programu ya Uthibitishaji — Kama Google Authenticator. Nambari zinabadilika kila sekunde 30. Nguvu.
3. Ufunguo wa Vifaa — Kama YubiKey. Inaunganishwa kwenye USB. Yenye nguvu zaidi.

Washa 2FA kwenye: barua pepe, M-Pesa, mitandao ya kijamii, na mifumo ya kazi.

MISSION BRIEFING: Before you take the oath of service and step onto the frontlines of the Civilization Map, understand the foundation and principles of the Rebuilder Corps.

The Rebuilder Corps was forged in the aftermath of The Blackout of 2031. When centralized institutions faltered, ordinary citizens — vocational trainees, network technicians, solar electricians, software developers, and university instructors — came together to rebuild East Africa's infrastructure. We are defined by three core tenets:

1. Sovereign Defense & Civic Service: We protect schools, hospitals, water supplies, and civic institutions. We never use our skills for illegal access, unauthorized hacking, or extortion.
2. Open Knowledge: Everything we learn is shared. Proprietary gatekeeping leaves communities vulnerable. We train each other, author open-source tools, and publish bilingual guides in English and Swahili.
3. Ethical & Legal Rigour: We operate strictly within the law — adhering to Kenya's Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act (CMCA 2018) and Data Protection Act (DPA 2019). We do not "hack back"; we defend, harden, and rebuild.

Wear your Corps designation with pride, whether you are a TVET apprentice or a senior systems engineer.

exercises.hint: This method requires physical possession of a device — impossible to SIM-swap.

options.text: SMS one-time password
Email one-time password
Authenticator app (TOTP)
Hardware security key (YubiKey)

exercises.prompt: Which 2FA method is most resistant to SIM-swap attacks?

Do not click — report the email as phishing and verify directly via the official KCB app or published number
Reply to the email asking for more information
Forward it to friends to warn them before deleting

An instructor has manually promoted you

exercises.explanation: FSRS tracks stability, difficulty, and due date per learner per concept. By scheduling review at the moment of near-forgetting, it achieves the same retention as cramming with a fraction of the study time.
exercises.hint: The algorithm watches your personal forgetting curve.

options.text: It is the fastest algorithm available
It schedules each review card at the optimal moment just before you would forget it, maximising retention per hour of study
It randomly selects cards to keep learners surprised
It focuses only on cards you have already mastered

exercises.prompt: Why does CyberLearn use the FSRS-4.5 spaced repetition algorithm for review sessions?

exercises.explanation: Reducing the reconnaissance yield, preparing staff for the expected phishing phase, and strengthening authentication are all high-impact, low-cost defences that directly counter the observed threat pattern.
exercises.hint: Reconnaissance is the first phase — you can make it harder and prepare for the likely next step (spear-phishing).

options.text: Shut down all hospital websites immediately
Remove staff names and roles from public websites, train staff to recognise spear-phishing, and enable 2FA on all email accounts
Wait until an actual attack occurs before responding
Change all passwords to the same strong password across all systems

exercises.explanation: An unpatched 2019 router has known critical vulnerabilities — it is the biggest external exposure. Unique passwords prevent credential stuffing. 2FA stops attackers who obtain a password. BYOD policy governance takes longest to enforce and comes last.
exercises.hint: Fix the perimeter first, then authentication, then policy.

options.text: Update router firmware → enforce unique passwords → enable 2FA on email → establish BYOD policy
Establish BYOD policy → update router firmware → enable 2FA → enforce unique passwords
Enable 2FA on email → enforce unique passwords → update router firmware → establish BYOD policy
All actions have equal priority and should be done simultaneously

exercises.prompt: You are assigned to secure a newly restored community health clinic network with shared passwords, no 2FA, unpatched router from 2019, and staff using personal phones for work email. Rank the actions by PRIORITY (first action first).
